To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the absorption of dietary fat in conventional animals is more affected by the deprivation of bile secretion than is fat absorption in germ-free animals, and that, in bile deprived conventional, but not germ-free, animals, the absorption of saturated fatty acids is more affected than the absorption of unsaturated fatty acids.

(1) the absorption of dietary fats in conventional animals is lower than in germ-free rats when bile secretion is artificially suppressed; (2) this difference is mainly due to a decrease in the absorption rate of saturated fatty acids; (3) the difference in the rate of fat absorption between germ-free and bile deprived conventional rats is due to a combination of factors including the biohydrogenation process of unsaturated fatty acids and the effect of bile deprivation on fat absorption.

the absorption of dietary fats is impaired in rats deprived of bile, that the extent of impairment is greater in conventional than in germ-free rats and that the difference in the extent of impairment cannot be explained by differences in the biohydrogenation rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the gastrointestinal flora in fat absorption in the rat.
the role of the intestinal microflora on fat digestion in conventional rats.
the effects of bile secretion deprivation in germ-free and in conventional rats on the absorption of fat and on the faecal excretions of fat and its constituents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of gastrointestinal flora in the conventional rat, as opposed to germ-free rats, results in an increase of the absorption of dietary fat and a decrease in the excretion of'soluble' lipids in the faeces.

the difference of fat digestion and absorption between germ-free and conventionally reared animals is not only due to a lack of microbial enzymes but also to a modification of digestive and absorptive processes in conventional animals as compared with germ-free ones.
bile is required for the efficient absorption of dietary lipoproteins in conventional rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of the gastrointestinal flora in the conventional animals is not essential to the absorption of fat but is essential to the absorption and metabolism of the bile secretions.
bile deprivation in conventional rats resulted in a significant reduction in fat absorption, whereas in germ-free rats, bile deprivation resulted only in a moderate reduction of fat absorption.

bile deprivation resulted in a decrease in the apparent absorption and a significant modification in the excretion of dietary lipids both in conventional and in germ-free animals, but that the effects were more pronounced in the former than in the latter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of the intestinal microbiota is not the only determinant for fat absorption in the small intestine.
the germ-free model can be useful for the study of the effects of bile secretion on fat absorption and faecal excretion in the absence of the gastrointestinal flora.
germ-free animals are less affected by bile deprivation than conventional animals.
